Let's talk about a phenomenon that anyone who has ever worked on a group project will recognize: social loafing. This is the tendency for people to put in less effort when they work as part of a group than when they work alone. The classic demonstration comes from a rope-pulling experiment in the late nineteenth century. An engineer noticed that when people pulled on a rope together, the total force was less than the sum of what each person could pull individually. Later researchers refined this with a clever design. They asked people to shout as loudly as they could, either alone or in a group, and they made people believe that their individual volume would not be measured. Group members consistently produced less noise than they did alone. Why? The main explanation is diffusion of responsibility. When the output is pooled, no one person's contribution can be identified, so each person feels less accountable. Now, this isn't inevitable. Researchers have found that social loafing shrinks when individual contributions are made visible, for example when each member's part of a project is graded separately. It also shrinks when the task is personally meaningful, or when the group is small and members know and respect each other. Interestingly, the effect also varies across cultures. In some cultures that emphasize collective goals, groups sometimes work harder than individuals, which is the opposite of what the original studies found. So the takeaway is not that groups are inherently lazy, but that group settings change the incentives people feel.

Cities are almost always warmer than the surrounding countryside, sometimes by several degrees, and this is called the urban heat island effect. There are a few contributing factors. First, there are the materials. Asphalt, concrete, and dark roofing absorb a large share of incoming sunlight and release it slowly after sunset, which is why a city can stay warm at night when the countryside has already cooled. Second, there's a lack of vegetation. Plants cool their surroundings by releasing water vapor, a process called transpiration, and by providing shade. In a downtown dominated by pavement, that cooling is largely absent. Third, the geometry of tall buildings traps heat. Streets lined with towers, what we call urban canyons, reduce the amount of heat that radiates back to the sky, and they slow the wind that might otherwise carry warm air away. Finally, there's waste heat from air conditioners, vehicles, and industry. Now, why should we care? Higher temperatures raise energy demand because of air conditioning, which in turn creates more waste heat, a kind of feedback loop. They also worsen air pollution and increase heat-related illness, especially among older residents. Some cities are responding with so-called cool roofs, which are painted white or covered with reflective coatings, and with green roofs planted with vegetation. Early studies suggest that cool roofs reduce indoor temperatures noticeably, though their effect on temperatures at street level is more modest. Green roofs help in both ways but cost considerably more to install.

Today I'd like to talk about how honey bees make honey. First, worker bees leave the hive and fly to flowers. They drink a sweet liquid called nectar and store it in a special stomach. When they return, they pass the nectar to other bees inside the hive. These bees chew the nectar for a while, and this changes it chemically. Then they place it in the small wax cells of the honeycomb. At this point, the nectar is still too wet. So the bees fan their wings to blow warm air over it, and the extra water slowly leaves. When the honey is thick enough, the bees cover the cell with a thin layer of wax. A hive can store enough honey to feed all the bees through the winter, when there are no flowers.

Long before clocks existed, people used the sun to tell the time. The simplest tool was the sundial. A sundial has a flat plate with numbers and a thin stick, called a gnomon, in the middle. When the sun shines, the stick makes a shadow on the plate. As the sun moves across the sky during the day, the shadow moves, too, and the number it touches shows the hour. Sundials were used in many ancient places, including Egypt, Greece, and China. But they had a problem. They did not work at night or on cloudy days. So later people invented water clocks, which measured time by the amount of water that dripped out of a container. Water clocks worked in any weather, but they were harder to build.

Today I want to talk about a rather humble organism, lichen, and why environmental scientists pay such close attention to it. A lichen isn't a single organism but a partnership between a fungus and an alga. The fungus provides structure and protection, while the alga produces food through photosynthesis. Now, here's what makes lichens useful. Unlike plants, they have no roots and no protective outer layer, so they absorb water and nutrients, and unfortunately pollutants, directly from the air over their entire surface. Sulfur dioxide, for instance, damages the alga, and the lichen dies. So if you went to an industrial city in nineteenth-century Britain, you'd find that the lichens near the factories had vanished, while those in the countryside were thriving. Researchers eventually turned that observation into a scale. Species that tolerate pollution, the crusty ones that hug tree bark, indicate heavily polluted air. Leafy species indicate moderate pollution, and bushy, hanging species survive only where the air is quite clean. Now, you might ask, why not just use an instrument? Well, instruments tell you what's in the air at the moment of measurement. Lichens, by contrast, record exposure over years. That said, they're not perfect. Lichens respond to many things, including humidity and the age of the tree, so a missing species doesn't automatically point to pollution. Scientists therefore use lichens as a first screening, and they follow up with chemical monitoring where the signs suggest trouble.

Let's start with a question that sounds almost childish: why is the sky dark at night? If the universe were infinite and filled evenly with stars, then in whichever direction you looked, your line of sight would eventually land on the surface of a star. The whole sky should blaze as brightly as the surface of the Sun. This puzzle is known as Olbers' paradox, after the nineteenth-century astronomer who popularized it, though it had been noticed earlier. For a long time, people proposed that dust between the stars absorbed the light. That doesn't work, I'm afraid. The dust would heat up and glow, so the energy would simply be re-emitted. The real solution came with the discovery that the universe isn't eternal. It has a finite age, roughly fourteen billion years. Light travels at a finite speed, so we can only see stars whose light has had time to reach us. Beyond that distance, there simply hasn't been time. That's the main reason. A second, smaller effect is that the universe is expanding, which stretches the light from distant galaxies to longer wavelengths and shifts some of it out of the visible range. Notice, by the way, that the darkness of the night sky was one of the earliest clues that the universe has a beginning. Next time, we'll look at how astronomers estimated that age.

The Puzzle of Yawning

Almost every vertebrate yawns, yet scientists still disagree about why. A popular explanation holds that yawning draws in extra oxygen, but experiments have undermined it: volunteers breathing air enriched with oxygen yawned just as often as those breathing normal air. A more recent proposal is that yawning helps cool the brain. Inhaling deeply sends cooler air past the blood vessels of the skull, and studies suggest that people yawn more in moderate temperatures than in very hot or very cold weather.

Yawning is also notably contagious. Seeing, hearing, or even reading about a yawn can trigger one, and the effect appears stronger among close friends and relatives than among strangers. This pattern has led some researchers to suggest that contagious yawning is linked to empathy, although the evidence is mixed: children under four rarely catch yawns, and some studies have found no difference between people with high and low empathy scores. For now, the simplest conclusion is that yawning probably serves more than one purpose.

The Bicycle

The first bicycle looked very different from the ones we ride today. In 1817, a German inventor built a wooden machine with two wheels but no pedals. Riders sat on it and pushed their feet against the ground to move forward. It was fun, but it was slow and tiring, and it was not popular for long.

Later, in the 1860s, French builders added pedals to the front wheel. These bicycles were heavy and uncomfortable, and people called them "boneshakers" because the roads were rough. In the 1880s, the "safety bicycle" appeared. It had two wheels of equal size and a chain that turned the back wheel. This design was easier and safer to ride, and it soon became popular around the world. Today, the basic shape of the bicycle has changed very little.

tasks.title: Read an Academic Passage
tasks.text:
Tacit Knowledge

In 1958 the philosopher Michael Polanyi observed that "we can know more than we can tell." A skilled cyclist keeps her balance by turning the handlebars slightly toward the direction in which she is falling, yet most cyclists could not state this rule, and those who can are no better at staying upright. Polanyi called such expertise tacit knowledge: competence that resides in practice rather than in propositions.

The notion posed a quiet challenge to engineers who hoped to codify skilled work. Efforts in the 1980s to capture the judgment of expert diagnosticians in software, for example, yielded systems that performed adequately on textbook cases but faltered on the ambiguous ones that experienced clinicians handle almost without noticing. Interviewing the experts did not help much; when pressed, they tended to offer plausible rationalizations that bore little relation to the cues they actually relied upon.

It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that tacit knowledge is mysterious or unteachable. Apprenticeship has transmitted it for millennia, not by explanation but by sustained proximity: novices watch, imitate, and are corrected in small ways until their judgments converge on those of the master. What resists transfer is not the knowledge itself but the shortcut of explicit instruction.

email.title: Write an Email
email.subject: Reference request for a scholarship
email.prompt:
Last summer, you completed an internship at a local marketing company. Your supervisor, Ms. Alvarez, gave you a lot of support and useful advice. You are now applying for a scholarship, and the application requires a reference letter from a recent supervisor.

Write an email to Ms. Alvarez. In your email, do the following:
- Thank her for something specific she did during your internship.
- Explain what the scholarship is and why you are applying.
- Ask whether she would write a reference letter, and give the deadline.

Use full sentences, and write as much as you can.
email.rubric: Task: polite request email to a former internship supervisor. Must cover all 3 bullets: (1) specific thanks (a task, skill or piece of advice, not generic), (2) what the scholarship is and why the writer applies, (3) a clear, courteous request for a reference with a deadline (and ideally an offer to send a CV or details). Look for appropriate register (warm but professional), greeting and sign-off, clear organization, accurate grammar and natural phrasing. Typical strong length 100-150 words.

discussion.title: Write for an Academic Discussion
discussion.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on economics. Post a reply to the professor's question. In your reply, do these two things.
- State your view and back it up.
- Add something new to the thread, in your own words.
Aim for at least 100 words.

professor.name: Dr. Nakamura
professor.text: This week we are studying 'nudges': small changes to how choices are presented that steer people toward better decisions without forbidding anything. Examples include automatically enrolling workers in a retirement savings plan unless they choose to leave it, or placing healthy food at eye level in school cafeterias. Supporters say nudges help people without limiting their freedom. Critics say governments should not try to steer people's decisions at all, even gently. Should governments use nudges? Why or why not?

students.name: Priya
students.text: I think nudges are a good idea. Automatic enrollment in retirement plans has greatly increased saving in some countries, and anyone who disagrees can still leave the plan. Nobody is forced to do anything, so I do not see the harm.

students.name: Marcus
students.text: I am uncomfortable with nudges. They work best when people do not notice them, which feels like manipulation. If the government wants people to eat better or save more, it should explain why openly and let people decide for themselves.

discussion.rubric: Task: academic discussion post, 100+ words. Look for a clear opinion on government nudges, specific support (examples, consequences, conditions), engagement with Priya's or Marcus's point rather than repeating it, coherence, varied accurate grammar and vocabulary.

interview.title: Take an Interview
interview.instructions: An interviewer will ask you four questions. There is no preparation time. Answer each question and use the whole time to say as much as you can.
interview.context: You are joining a research study about work experience and career preparation. A researcher will ask you some questions in a short online interview.

items.text: Thanks for taking part. To begin, can you tell me about a job, internship, or volunteer role you've had, and what you did there?
Some people learn best at work by watching experienced colleagues, while others prefer to learn by trying things on their own. Which way works better for you, and why?

Many companies offer internships that are unpaid. Some people say this is fair because interns gain valuable experience. Others say it is unfair to students who cannot afford to work for free. What is your view?

Final question. Some universities are considering making an internship a requirement for graduation in every major, including subjects like history and philosophy. Do you think this is a good idea? Why or why not?
